There is a procedure for after. It is long. It is also, the manual insists, the important part.

choices.text: Full inspection, every panel

outcome.narrative: Every panel, every seam, every weld the shots came near. You find two problems nobody had noticed and fix them before they could be noticed the hard way. The ship feels sturdier. So does the crew.

choices.text: Patch what is obvious and keep moving

outcome.narrative: The viewport seal gets resealed and the toast-smelling loom gets a strip of tape and a stern look. The rest can wait. The rest, as a rule, does not like waiting.

choices.text: Let the crew talk it through first

outcome.narrative: Everyone sits in the galley and says what they saw. It takes two days. Nobody is fixing anything during those two days, and they are the most useful days of the voyage.

title: Load-Bearing Luggage

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has measured the hold and found it is 100% full of OPPORTUNITY! Also crates! Mostly crates!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has run every packing configuration. There are 4,812. They all hold exactly the same amount, which is the amount you already have.
ai_flavor.rex: REX considers the hold a fortified position. Fully stocked. Defensible. He would like the crew to stop sleeping on the ammunition crates, which are not ammunition crates.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can offer you more cargo space with a CHIP Storage Plus subscription! The subscription does not change the size of the ship! It changes how you feel about it!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY said at the last station that you did not need the third crate of that. She will not say which crate. You know which crate.

body:
The hold is full. Not nearly full. Full, in the sense that the door now closes only if someone leans on it, and the someone has to be heavy.

Crates have migrated into the corridors. A sack of something is wedged behind the galley stove. One crew member has started using a box of spare filters as a nightstand and describes it as "the best thing that has happened to me."

Someone suggests reorganizing.

choices.text: Reorganize the hold properly

outcome.narrative: Two days of lifting, labeling, and arguing about labels. When it is done, everything fits exactly as well as it did before, but now it is alphabetical. You will still have to drop something to pick anything up.

choices.text: Declare the corridors official storage

outcome.narrative: The corridors are now cargo. The crew learns to walk sideways and develops strong opinions about who left the sack there. The filter-box nightstand is formally recognized. The hold remains full.

title: Ballroom

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has never seen the hold floor before! It is beige! ARIA loves beige! ARIA has announced a dance!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes that an empty hold is either a sign of efficient trading or of having nothing left to trade. He has looked at the books. He will not be specifying.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has repurposed the empty hold as a drill floor. Nobody has attended a drill. Three people have attended a dance, which REX insists was a drill.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has detected unused capacity! Unused capacity is a missed revenue opportunity! CHIP has rented the hold to nobody, for free, as a loss leader!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY is not saying the hold is empty because of choices. She is saying the hold is empty, and that choices exist, and that you may connect those however you like.

body:
The hold is empty. Completely: no crates, no sacks, no mystery cylinder somebody swore was important. Just a large, cold, echoing room with good lighting and a clean floor.

The crew keeps finding reasons to walk through it. Someone tried a cartwheel. Someone else timed it.

It is, by a wide margin, the biggest space aboard.

choices.text: Hold a dance in the hold

outcome.narrative: There is no band, so the crew claps the rhythm and argues about the tempo. It is the worst dance anyone has attended and nobody leaves early. The cartwheel record falls twice.

choices.text: Seal it off to save on air

outcome.narrative: You seal the empty hold and stop heating and cycling a room with nothing in it. The air budget improves slightly. The crew stands at the sealed door for a moment, as if at a closed park.

title: Sleet

ai_flavor.aria: Space glitter! ARIA has always wanted to see it up close! It is coming up VERY close!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV puts the stream at nine hours wide on this heading. Each grain carries the energy of a thrown stone. He has multiplied. He wishes he hadn't.
ai_flavor.rex: REX recommends presenting the armored bow and taking the fire. You do not outrun artillery. You outlast it.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that micrometeoroid damage is an Act of Cosmos under your policy! Acts of Cosmos are not covered! Very little is covered!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY would have plotted around the stream when it first showed on long-range. She did mention it. It's in the log, under 'things nobody reads.'

body:
The forward sensors report grit. Then more grit. Then a word the sensor log has never used before, which turns out to be 'sleet.'

A debris stream — sand-sized, fast, and in no particular hurry to end — is crossing your heading. Individually, each grain is nothing. The ship is about to meet several billion individuals.

choices.text: Pilot threads the gaps

outcome.narrative: The pilot reads the stream like weather, sliding the ship through its thin places on short, expensive burns. A few grains get through anyway. The paint keeps most of its opinions.

choices.text: Patch the thin plates first

outcome.narrative: You slap patches on the thinnest plates before the stream arrives. The sleet hisses across the ship for nine hours and finds almost nothing worth the effort. The patch tray is lighter.

choices.text: Bow into it and take the sleet

outcome.narrative: You turn the armored bow into the stream and let it hiss against the plating for nine hours. The hull takes a scouring. The forward water tank, which sits behind the bow plating for exactly this reason, takes the rest: a seam opens and weeps {cost.water} points before anyone finds it. The forward viewport now looks like frosted glass, artistically.

choices.text: Go the long way around

outcome.narrative: The detour is wide and slow and burns what detours burn: fuel, and {cost.food} points of food for no distance at all. The stream passes harmlessly to port, glittering, as though it was never interested.

alt_bodies:
The forward camera picks up a glitter across the dark, like frost on a window that isn't there. The sensor log, after some thought, files it under 'sleet.'

It is a debris stream: grains no bigger than sand, moving fast, spread wide, and crossing your heading for longer than anyone wants to estimate. No single grain matters. The hull is about to meet all of them.

The navigation plot grows a gray smear right where the ship is going. Close up, the smear is sand. Fast sand, a whole river of it, which the sensor log, for want of a better word, calls 'sleet.'

Each grain on its own would bounce off the paint. There are not going to be any grains on their own. The stream is in no hurry to end, and the ship is in its path.

title: The Reclaimer Coughs

ai_flavor.aria: An indoor water feature! ARIA has always said this ship needed more ambiance!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the loss rate. At this pace the reclaimer is dry in nine days. He has also, unasked, worked out how long the crew lasts after that. It is the shorter number.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has sealed the crawlspace hatch in case the leak is hostile. He accepts that leaks are not hostile. The hatch stays sealed.
ai_flavor.chip: Water loss is covered under AquaCare™ Plus! You have AquaCare™! The Plus was the part that covered things!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY flagged that seal at the last service. She isn't saying 'told you.' She'd just like 'told you' entered in the log as a formal observation.

body:
The water reclaimer makes a noise like a man clearing his throat before bad news, and then delivers it: a pump seal has failed, and the loop is emptying into a crawlspace that was not designed to hold anything.

The crawlspace is filling. The reclaimer is emptying. There is a direct relationship between these two facts, and nobody likes it.

choices.text: Engineer swaps the seal

outcome.narrative: The engineer crawls in, swaps the seal, crawls out, and wrings a sleeve out over the reclaimer intake, on principle. Some of the water is gone for good. The rest is back where it belongs.

choices.text: Print a replacement seal

outcome.narrative: The fabricator turns out a seal in the wrong color and roughly the right shape. It holds. The fabricator sounds tired afterwards, and the crawlspace dries out in its own time.

choices.text: Bail it back by hand — all hands

outcome.narrative: Everyone takes a bucket. The crawlspace is bailed back into the loop one indignity at a time. The water comes back, mostly. The dignity does not.

choices.text: Bypass the loop and ration

outcome.narrative: You bypass the reclaimer and put the crew on rations until a station can sell you a seal. The crawlspace stays full. The tanks don't.

alt_bodies:
There is water in the crawlspace under the reclaimer, which is the wrong place for water to be. A pump seal has failed, and the loop is draining into the dark one steady trickle at a time.

The reclaimer's gauge goes down. The crawlspace goes up. The ship has invented a second, worse water tank.

Someone goes to fetch a spanner from the crawlspace and comes back wet to the knee. A pump seal on the water reclaimer has split, and the loop has been quietly emptying itself under the deck plates.

The crawlspace was built for cables. It is now full of water. The tanks were built for water, and are now full of less of it.

title: Cabin Fever

ai_flavor.aria: The crew is having FEELINGS! Together! Sort of together! ARIA is counting this as team-building!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV traced the mug. It was in the growbay the whole time. Telling anyone would end this feud and start a worse one about who left it there.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has drawn up a crew separation plan with patrol schedules for the galley. Nobody has asked for it. It is ready anyway.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP offers ConflictBuddy™ mediation, billed per grievance! Early estimates suggest this crew is very billable!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY saw this coming at the second mention of the mug. She'd have stepped in then. She's stepping in now, which is later, which is your schedule, not hers.

body:
Nobody aboard is speaking to anybody. It started with two people and spread, in solidarity, though nobody is sure with whom.

It began with a missing mug. It is no longer about the mug. The galley rota has become a treaty, and the treaty has become a border.

choices.text: Chef cooks a peace dinner

outcome.narrative: The chef cooks something out of nothing, which is the chef's whole job, and seats the feud at opposite ends of the same bench. By the second course they are complaining about the chef together. The chef considers this a success, and is correct.

choices.text: Break out the good rations

outcome.narrative: The good rations come out and the galley table fills back up. Nobody discusses the mug. Everyone discusses the food. The border dissolves somewhere around dessert, and so does a week of stores.

choices.text: Call a meeting and hash it out

outcome.narrative: It takes two days, three apologies, one walkout and every biscuit aboard, because nobody can hold a meeting without them. The mug is found. The treaty is dissolved. Everyone is a little worse off and a little closer, which is most of what a crew is.

choices.text: Let them sort it out themselves

outcome.narrative: You let it run. It runs through the ship for a week, on separate sittings with separate pots and twice the waste, and settles, as these things do, on one person, who takes the brunt of it and says nothing. That is not the same as it being over.

alt_bodies:
The galley now has two sittings, which nobody scheduled, and two kettles, which nobody bought. Nobody aboard is speaking to anybody else, on principle, and everyone is vague about which principle.

It was a mug, once. It has become a treaty, with clauses, and the treaty has a border running down the middle of the galley table.

Somebody's mug went missing a week ago. It has not been found, and it has stopped mattering, because the argument outgrew it.

The crew now talk only through the ship computer, which has lately stopped passing the messages on. The galley rota reads like a treaty. The table has a border. Nobody remembers drawing it.

title: The Toll Lane

ai_flavor.aria: A TOLL BOOTH! In SPACE! ARIA has never paid a toll! ARIA would love to pay a toll!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has checked the toll beacon's license. It expired nine years ago. The beacon is collecting anyway. He notes that nobody has come to stop it, and that nobody will.
ai_flavor.rex: REX notes the toll booth has no weapons. It has a very firm voice. He is not going to argue with the voice.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has a frequent-traveler card for this toll! It has lapsed! CHIP is deeply sorry! CHIP is also proud it ever had one!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says pay and keep the hull, or keep the gold and take the rocks. Or, with a good hand at the helm, slip past it. She didn't say your hand.

body:
The fork has a toll booth.

It's a beacon the size of a shipping container, parked in the mouth of the port lane, broadcasting a price list. The port lane is marked {branch.alpha.label}; its first stop reads as {branch.alpha.first}. The starboard lane, marked {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, has no toll. It has a debris field instead, which is cheaper, and louder.

choices.text: Pay the toll: port lane

outcome.narrative: You pay. The beacon thanks you warmly, issues a receipt and raises a barrier that is entirely symbolic. The port lane is clear and quiet and smells, somehow, of tarmac.

choices.text: Take the free lane: starboard, through the debris

outcome.narrative: You take the free lane and the debris field that comes with it. It rattles the hull for a long hour. Four points of hull. The toll beacon wishes you a pleasant journey as you pass, in a tone that suggests it doesn't mean it.

choices.text: The pilot slips past the booth

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} waits for the beacon's scanner to sweep the other way and slides through the gap behind it at a speed the beacon has no rule for. It sends an invoice anyway, to an address that has been closed for years. The crew finds this very satisfying.

title: Lane Closed for Works

ai_flavor.aria: ROADWORKS! In SPACE! Someone is FIXING space! ARIA had no idea space could be fixed! ARIA wants to watch!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates the works have progressed eleven meters in fourteen years. At this rate the lane will reopen in about two thousand years. The long way round costs fuel. The slow zone costs days.
ai_flavor.rex: REX notes the drone is unarmed and slow. It is the least threatening thing he has seen this trip. He is suspicious of it on principle.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP knows the contractor! They won the bid! They have been winning the bid for fourteen years! CHIP admires them enormously!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says crawl through the works and lose two days, or go round and burn the fuel. Neither is wrong. She'd just like to see which one you talk yourself into.

body:
The fork has roadworks.

A string of orange beacons blocks most of the port lane, which is marked {branch.alpha.label} and leads first to {branch.alpha.first}. A maintenance drone is working in it, very slowly, on something nobody can see. A sign says SLOW · WORKS AHEAD · 12 DAYS. The sign is fourteen years old.

The starboard lane, {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, is open, but it's the long way round.

choices.text: Crawl through the works: port lane

outcome.narrative: You crawl through the slow zone at the posted speed, which is barely faster than standing still, past the drone, which does not look up. It takes two days. Nobody aboard has ever been this bored. The lane on the far side is, at least, very smooth.

choices.text: Go the long way: starboard lane

outcome.narrative: You go round. The starboard lane is open, empty and long, and the extra distance burns four points of fuel. Behind you, the maintenance drone carries on with whatever it is doing, the way it has for fourteen years.

choices.text: The engineer offers the drone a hand

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} gets on the drone's channel, works out what it has been trying to fix, and sends it the part number it needed fourteen years ago. The drone finishes the job in two days and switches off the beacons. You're the first ship through the port lane in fourteen years. The drone plays you a little tune.

alt_bodies:
Someone is mending the fork.

The port lane, marked {branch.alpha.label}, first stop {branch.alpha.first}, is fenced with orange beacons. A lone maintenance drone floats in the middle of it, welding something invisible with enormous care. A sign reads SLOW · WORKS AHEAD. It has been reading that since before anyone aboard learned to fly.

The starboard lane, marked {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, has no works in it and a great deal more of it: open, clear, and long.

The port lane has cones in it.

Orange beacons, strictly, strung across the lane marked {branch.alpha.label}, the way to {branch.alpha.first}, around a maintenance drone that is fixing something slowly and alone. The works sign beside it has faded almost blank, which takes a very long time out here.

Starboard, the lane marked {branch.beta.label} runs clear to {branch.beta.first}. It just takes the long way round to do it.

title: Both Lanes Watched

ai_flavor.aria: PIRATES! Or a STORM! ARIA likes neither of them! ARIA would like a third option! ARIA has been told there isn't one!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the picket's demand at roughly a tenth of the cargo. The storm's hull damage is harder to estimate. He has estimated it. He does not like the estimate.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has the picket on the scope. Two ships, light weapons, heavy attitude. He could fight them. He would rather not, on a fork, with a storm next door.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP must point out that pirate tolls are not tax deductible! CHIP has asked! The pirates laughed! It was a very rude laugh!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the storm only takes hull. The pirates take what they like, unless someone talks them down. She'd send the diplomat, if anyone asked her.

body:
Both lanes ahead are a problem.

The port lane, marked {branch.alpha.label}, first stop {branch.alpha.first}, has a pirate picket sitting in its mouth: two armed ships, engines idling, a polite request on the open channel for a share of whatever you're carrying. The starboard lane, marked {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, has no pirates in it, because it has a dust storm in it, and pirates aren't stupid.

There is no third lane. The ship computer has looked.

choices.text: Pay the picket: port lane

outcome.narrative: You pay. The pirates take a share of the food and water, call it fair, and wave you through with something close to courtesy. The port lane beyond them is quiet. The galley is quieter.

choices.text: Run the storm: starboard lane

outcome.narrative: You take the storm. It sandblasts the ship for six hours: grit in the vents, static on every channel, the hull hissing like a kettle. Ten points of hull. The pirates, safe in their lane, watch you go in and do not follow.

choices.text: The diplomat talks the picket down

outcome.narrative: {crew.diplomat} opens a channel and talks to the picket for an hour about the price of fuel, the weather, and the many other ships that will be along shortly with richer cargoes. The pirates settle for a token, a crate of rations, and let you through laughing. The diplomat refuses to say what the joke was.

alt_bodies:
Neither lane ahead is good news.

In the mouth of the port lane, marked {branch.alpha.label}, first stop {branch.alpha.first}, two armed ships sit with their engines idling and a recorded message on loop, politely requesting a share of whatever you're carrying. The starboard lane, marked {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, is empty of pirates. It is full of dust storm, which is why it is empty of pirates.

The ship computer has checked for a third option, twice, in case it missed one.

The fork offers a choice of problems.

Port, the lane marked {branch.alpha.label} toward {branch.alpha.first}: a pirate picket, two ships, guns warm, and a voice on the open channel explaining, with great courtesy, that a share of your cargo will be required. Starboard, the lane marked {branch.beta.label} toward {branch.beta.first}: a dust storm churning across the whole lane, which the pirates have very sensibly declined to sit in.

The chart shows no third lane. The chart has been asked more than once.

title: The Closing Gap

ai_flavor.aria: The gap is CLOSING! Like a DOOR! ARIA would like to go through the door! ARIA would like to go through it NOW!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV puts the port gap at forty minutes from closing. The ship can make it in thirty. Ten minutes is a margin. It is not a large one. The long way is safe and costs fuel and days.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has calculated the gap's closing speed. It is slow. It is also two rocks the size of cities. He would not like to be between them for the last of it.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's navigation subscription would have warned you about this! It was canceled for non-payment! CHIP is just mentioning it! At a very bad time!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says if you're going through, go now and don't hesitate. Otherwise go round and don't look back. Hesitating is the one option she'd rule out, and you're doing it now.

body:
The fork is a pair of gaps between two drifting rocks, and one of them is closing.

The port gap, marked {branch.alpha.label}, first stop {branch.alpha.first}, is narrowing by the minute as the two rocks drift together. It is still wide enough, now. It will not be in an hour. The starboard route, marked {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, goes all the way round the outside of both rocks: open, safe, and long.

choices.text: Shoot the closing gap: port

outcome.narrative: You burn hard for the gap and make it with minutes to spare, the rock faces close enough on either side to read the strata. The hull scrapes once near the end, a long grinding note. Six of fuel, six of hull. Behind you, an hour later, the gap closes with a silent shudder that rings the field for days.

choices.text: Go round the outside: starboard

outcome.narrative: You go round. It takes four days and five points of fuel to circle both rocks, by which time the gap has closed behind you and the field is quiet again. Nobody was squashed. That was the point.

choices.text: The pilot threads it at full speed

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} takes the gap at a speed nobody aboard would have chosen, straight down the middle, without a scratch. Eight points of fuel for the burn. The crew comes out the far side cheering, and the pilot pretends that wasn't the plan all along.

alt_bodies:
Two rocks the size of small moons are drifting into each other, very slowly, and the fork runs between them.

The port gap, marked {branch.alpha.label}, first stop {branch.alpha.first}, is still open. It is narrower than when you first saw it, and it will be shut within the hour. The starboard route, marked {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, goes the long way round the outside of both rocks, where nothing is closing on anything.

The fork is a door, and the door is shutting.

Between the two drifting rocks, the port gap, marked {branch.alpha.label}, first stop {branch.alpha.first}, narrows as you watch: wide enough for the ship now, wide enough for nothing in an hour. The starboard route, marked {branch.beta.label}, first stop {branch.beta.first}, swings wide round both rocks. It is safe, open, and very long.

title: Halfway

ai_flavor.aria: HALFWAY! We're HALFWAY! ARIA made the banner! ARIA was asked not to say! ARIA has said!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the midpoint by distance. By time it was two days ago. He has decided not to mention that.
ai_flavor.rex: REX notes halfway means the same distance in either direction. He will not be suggesting the other direction.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has a Halfway Celebration Package! It contains a banner! You already have a banner! CHIP is offering a second banner!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says let them have it. She'd have skipped the second exclamation mark, but nobody consulted her on the banner.

body:
The navigation display ticks over to 50%.

Half of the trail is behind you. Half is ahead. It is, technically, just another number on a screen. The crew has decided it is not just another number on a screen. There is a banner in the galley that says HALFWAY!!, with two exclamation marks, which nobody will admit to having made.

choices.text: Break out the good rations

outcome.narrative: You open the sealed crate of good rations, the one with the real chocolate in it, and the halfway party runs late into third watch. It costs {cost.food} points of food. Nobody regrets a crumb of it.

choices.text: A small toast, then back to work

outcome.narrative: Everyone crowds into the galley for five minutes and raises whatever they're drinking at the banner. Somebody makes a short speech. Then back to work, with the banner left up, which is the right amount of celebration for half of something.

choices.text: Mark it on the airlock door and keep going

outcome.narrative: You scratch a line on the inside of the airlock door at eye height, with the date, and carry on. It isn't much of a ceremony. By the end of the week there are more initials beside it.

alt_bodies:
The navigation display reaches the halfway mark.

Half the trail done, half still to do. On paper it is one more reading among a great many. The crew has overruled the paper. A banner has gone up in the galley, reading HALFWAY in letters that get smaller towards the end, where the writer ran out of room. Nobody will say who made it.

Halfway. The nav display says so, and then, because somebody in the crew got there first, so does the galley.

There is a banner over the galley table, made from a bedsheet and a marker pen, reading HALFWAY, with the second A drawn slightly bigger than the first, for emphasis. Nobody has claimed it. It is, technically, just a point on a line. Nobody aboard is treating it that way.

title: Past the Point

ai_flavor.aria: Turning back was never the plan! ARIA is fine! ARIA is absolutely fine! ARIA would like a moment!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has run the return figures four times. The answer has not improved. It is, he notes, the first time a sum has made him feel anything.
ai_flavor.rex: REX notes there is no retreat. He has never favored retreat. He finds he would have liked the option.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP regrets that this voyage is now non-refundable! It always was! It's just more noticeable now!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says tell them, straight and now. Otherwise they'll find out from the fuel gauge, and then they'll ask why you didn't.

body:
The ship computer asks for a private word on the bridge.

It has done the sum it does every day, and today the answer has changed: there is no longer enough fuel to turn round and get home. Not at any pace, not with any luck. From here on, the only way out of this voyage is through it.

It thought you should know first. It would like to know who else you'd like to know.

choices.text: Gather the crew and say it plainly

outcome.narrative: You call everyone to the galley and tell them straight: no turning back from here. There is a silence. Then somebody says 'well, I wasn't going to,' and someone laughs, and it turns into the best evening the ship has had in a while.

choices.text: The pilot re-plots with what you know now

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} spends two days re-plotting the rest of the route from scratch, with every lesson of the first half folded in. The new line is tighter than the old one, and the fuel it saves is real. The point of no return is still behind you, but the way forward is a little shorter.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself

outcome.narrative: You keep it to yourself. It sits with you, heavy, at every meal. The crew can tell something's wrong. They don't know what. That turns out to be worse.

alt_bodies:
The ship computer asks if you have a moment, alone, on the bridge.

It runs the same check every morning, and every morning until now the answer was yes. Today it is no: the tank can no longer carry the ship back home, at any speed, with any luck. The only way out of the voyage now is to finish it.

It wanted you to hear it first. It asks who else should hear it.

The bridge is empty except for you and the ship computer, which is how the ship computer asked for it.

It has crossed a line in its daily arithmetic. Until today there was always enough fuel to turn round. There isn't now, and there won't be again. Home is no longer a direction the ship can go. Forward is the only one left.

It told you first. It is waiting to hear who else should be told.

title: Something Left Behind

ai_flavor.aria: No COFFEE? ARIA doesn't drink coffee! ARIA is panicking on everyone's behalf!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV estimates turning back costs two days and some fuel. Not turning back costs morale, compounded daily, for months. He has graphed it. The graph is not encouraging.
ai_flavor.rex: REX does not drink coffee. REX is aware he is in a minority of one. He is keeping his opinions to himself, for his own safety.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's Bean There loyalty card has eleven stamps! The twelfth is free! The twelfth is on the dock!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the fabricator can print something coffee-shaped. It won't be coffee. It might be close enough. She'd have checked the pallet, personally.

body:
The galley inventory comes back with one line missing.

The coffee is not aboard. The entire supply, every sealed tin of it, is sitting on a pallet on the departure dock, where it was put down 'just for a second' during loading. The ship has tea. Nobody on the ship drinks tea. The next coffee is a very long way away.

choices.text: Turn back for it

outcome.narrative: You turn back. It costs time, fuel and a very embarrassing hail to the departure dock, where the coffee is waiting exactly where it was left. The crew greets the pallet like a returning hero. Nobody mentions the detour ever again.

choices.text: Print a substitute on the fabricator

outcome.narrative: The fabricator prints something brown, granular and roughly coffee-adjacent out of the ship's organic stores. It is not coffee. It is hot and bitter and it comes in a cup, and by the third week the crew insists it's better than the real thing, which is a lie everyone agrees to.

choices.text: Do without

outcome.narrative: You do without. The first week is grim. The second week, someone discovers the tea is quite good, actually. By the third week there is a tea rota, and a tea faction, and the coffee is never spoken of again.

title: The Schedule Meeting

ai_flavor.aria: We're LATE! ARIA hates being late! ARIA has never been late before! ARIA has never been anywhere before!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV puts the ship roughly a sixth of the deadline behind its distance. At this pace it keeps slipping. One bad stop and it slips faster. A faster pace closes it with room to spare, at the cost of fuel and tempers.
ai_flavor.rex: REX recommends speed. REX always recommends speed. This time he has the figures.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that the colony charter's late-arrival clause is very strict! CHIP has read it! It's mostly the word 'forfeit'!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says pick a pace you can hold this time. A fast pace you give up on halfway is just a slow pace with extra steps. She has seen your extra steps.

body:
The ship computer has put the deadline on the main screen in the galley, which it only does when it wants a meeting.

The numbers are simple. You have used more of the time than you have flown of the trail. Not disastrously, yet. But the gap is growing, and the colony slot will not wait for a ship that arrives late, however good its reasons.

Everybody has an opinion. Most of the opinions involve going faster.

choices.text: Burn harder from here

outcome.narrative: You order the pace up a notch, effective now. The drive note rises, the fuel gauge starts falling faster, and the crew settles in for a harder, shorter voyage. The gap on the galley screen starts, slowly, to close.

choices.text: Burn harder, and cut rations to pay for it

outcome.narrative: Faster pace and short rations both, effective now: the food you save pays for the fuel you burn, more or less. The crew grumbles at the vending-machine meals and gets on with it. The gap on the screen starts closing at once.

choices.text: Accept it. Arrive late, arrive whole

outcome.narrative: You keep the pace as it is. Better to arrive late than not at all, you tell them, and some of them agree. The deadline stays on the galley screen anyway, ticking, where everyone can see it at every meal.

title: Cutting Corners

ai_flavor.aria: The FOOTNOTE pace! ARIA has always wanted to see the footnote pace! ARIA has also read the footnote! ARIA is less keen!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the footnote. It describes the fastest pace as 'not recommended for sustained use.' He notes 'sustained' is undefined. He suspects whoever drew the diagram noticed that too.
ai_flavor.rex: REX approves of speed. He disapproves of the rattle. He is holding both positions firmly.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's warranty is void at the footnote pace! CHIP would like to stress the warranty was already void! For other reasons! Several!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says decide now. Every stop you spend thinking about it costs the time you're trying to save. She'll wait. That's the problem.

body:
A proposal has turned up on the bridge, with a diagram, which is never a good sign.

The ship is behind, and falling further behind. The proposal is to stop being careful about it: fly hard, skip the maintenance stops, run the drive at a pace the manual describes only in a footnote. It will get you there. It will get you there tired, short of fuel and with a ship that rattles.

The alternative is to arrive after the slot is gone.

choices.text: Plaid, and don't look back

outcome.narrative: PLAID, effective now. The drive goes up to a pitch you can feel in your teeth and stays there. Fuel burns like paper. Everybody sleeps badly. The gap on the deadline screen shrinks every single day, and nobody aboard has ever been so glad to watch a number.

choices.text: One notch faster, and keep the maintenance

outcome.narrative: You compromise: one notch faster, and you spend a little fuel on a proper drive service first so the ship can take it. The diagram's margin now calls it the coward's footnote. The ship stops rattling. The gap starts closing.

choices.text: Let it go. You'll get there when you get there

outcome.narrative: You turn the proposal down. The diagram goes back in its folder without a word. The ship flies on at the pace it was flying, the gap on the screen keeps growing, and the crew starts doing the sum in their heads at dinner.

title: Delivery Day

ai_flavor.aria: The LETTERS! We're nearly there with the LETTERS! ARIA has checked on them every single morning! They're fine! They're still letters!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has counted the colony's registry against the envelopes. One hundred and ninety-one of the addressees are on it. The other twenty-three are addressed to 'anyone.' He thinks that might be the most important pile.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has guarded the box since the station. He would like it noted that not one letter was lost. He would like that noted in the log, permanently.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP would like to waive the delivery fee! There was never a delivery fee! CHIP is waiving it anyway! It feels wonderful!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says send the names ahead. She has had the list formatted since the station, waiting on you. People should get to wait for something good for once.

body:
The colony's comms are in range for the first time.

And so, in the hold, is the dockmaster's box: two hundred and fourteen letters, still sealed, from people who never got a berth to people who did. You could transmit the names ahead now, so the colony knows they're coming. You could wait and hand them over in person when you land. The box seems heavier than it did, sitting there, so close to where it's going.

choices.text: Transmit the names ahead

outcome.narrative: You send the colony the list of names. Within the hour the replies start coming back: people who had given up on hearing from home, asking if it's really true, asking when you land, asking you to say thank you to someone at a station they'll never see. The crew reads the replies aloud at dinner. Some of them have to stop partway through.

choices.text: Read the 'to anyone' letters to the crew

outcome.narrative: You open the twenty-three letters addressed to 'anyone' (they were written for whoever found them, after all) and read them aloud to the crew over one long evening. Messages from strangers on a dying planet, to strangers on a new one. Everyone aboard counts as anyone. Everyone listens.

choices.text: Keep them sealed and deliver by hand

outcome.narrative: You keep the box sealed. Some things should be handed over in person, and you will. The crew agrees, without much discussion, that the box will be the first thing off the ship.

title: The Inspectors

ai_flavor.aria: They want to SEE the sparkly crop! ARIA knew it would be famous! ARIA has been practicing its introduction!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes the agronomists sound curious, not hostile. A crop that grows a third better is the kind of thing colonies hope for. He would show them everything.
ai_flavor.rex: REX notes there are four of them. He has reviewed them. Unarmed. Very enthusiastic. He has seen worse inspections.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP would like to point out that this is exactly what CHIP said would happen! CHIP did not say this! CHIP is going to say it now!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says tell them the truth, all of it. It's a good story. She'd tell it better, but go on.

body:
The colony's agronomists hail you before you're even in orbit.

They've seen your manifest. They've also seen the growbay readings you sent ahead, and the readings don't match the manifest: a silver-veined crop, healthier than anything that has arrived in years, which is not the crop the colony asked for. They have questions. There are four of them on the call. All of them sound like people who have spent their lives on exactly this kind of question, and have been waiting for one this interesting.

choices.text: Show them everything

outcome.narrative: You send them every reading, every log and every picture of the silver plants, from the first strange leaf onward. They go very quiet, then very loud. By the time you land they have cleared space in the colony's main greenhouse for it, and they meet the growbay at the airlock with gloves on.

choices.text: The diplomat makes the case

outcome.narrative: {crew.diplomat} takes the call and makes the case: what the crop was, what it became, and what it might mean for a colony that needs every advantage. By the end the agronomists are arguing with each other about where to plant it first. The crop is not on the manifest. It is now at the top of it.

choices.text: Let them take samples on arrival

outcome.narrative: You agree to let them sample it when you land. They take a great many samples. The crop arrives a little thinner than it left the growbay, and very famous.

title: The Jar

ai_flavor.aria: It GREW! It actually GREW! ARIA said it would! ARIA said it would at least four hundred times!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV revises the node's odds. They were one in twenty. They are now one in one. He has never been so happy to have been wrong in the correct direction.
ai_flavor.rex: REX stands down the guard on the node. The node is now a plant. Plants are not his department. He is staying anyway.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is restoring the crop warranty! Retroactively! For the whole voyage! CHIP has no authority! CHIP has never cared less!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says plant it first. Before anything else is unloaded. The colony can wait five minutes. She has waited longer than that for most of your decisions.

body:
The jar on the bridge has a leaf in it.

One leaf, small and pale and new, unfolding out of the green node cut from the dead crop all those stops ago. Nobody saw it happen. It was simply there one morning, as the colony's lights came up on the long-range scope. Nobody aboard has stopped looking at it.

choices.text: Plant it first thing

outcome.narrative: Before the cargo, before the crew, before anything else comes off the ship, you carry the jar down the ramp and plant the little leaf in the colony's first bed. A small crowd gathers. Nobody explains it to them. They work it out.

choices.text: Give it to the colony's seed bank

outcome.narrative: You hand the jar to the colony's seed bank, where the people who will look after it know exactly what they're looking at. They give it its own label and its own shelf. The label says what crop it came from, and what ship.

choices.text: Keep it on the bridge a little longer

outcome.narrative: You keep the jar on the bridge for the last leg in, where everyone can see it. There's no hurry. It has come this far. It can come the rest of the way with the crew.

title: Looking Back

ai_flavor.aria: A SELFIE with HOME! ARIA has wanted to do this for ages! Everybody squeeze in! Home, squeeze in!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes the camera faces forward because nothing dangerous comes from behind. He concedes that is not the only reason to look.
ai_flavor.rex: REX does not look back. It was in his training. He would like somebody to tell him what the picture looks like.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can offer the picture as a framed print, a mug or a commemorative blanket! The blanket is mostly black! Very slimming!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says people keep a picture of where they came from for the days they forget why they left. She isn't saying you forget things. She's saying take the picture.

body:
The ship computer mentions, over breakfast, that nobody has looked back since departure.

It means it literally. The long-range camera has pointed forward the whole way, because that is where things come from. It could point the other way. Home is still back there. It checked.

A proper picture means swinging the whole ship round and flying backwards for two days, which costs fuel. The rear camera can manage without turning, badly, through the engine glare. Or there is the hull survey, which is overdue, and does not require anybody to feel anything.

choices.text: Turn the ship round for a proper picture

outcome.narrative: The ship swings round on its thrusters and flies backwards for two whole days. The picture, when it comes, is mostly black, with home in it, smaller than anyone expected. Somebody prints it and pins it in the galley, and people touch it on the way past without meaning to.

log_lore.title: THE PICTURE
log_lore.text:
Pinned up in the galley, under the picture, somebody has written in marker: 'Everyone we know is in this one.'

It has been done before. Long ago a probe on its way out of the solar system was turned round, at the request of an astronomer who had to argue for it, to take a last family portrait of the planets. Earth came out as less than a single pixel, caught in a band of scattered sunlight. He called it a pale blue dot, and wrote that everyone who had ever lived had lived there.

Ours came out a little different. It still counts.

choices.text: Make do with the rear camera

outcome.narrative: The rear camera, which mostly watches the engine, takes a grainy picture past the exhaust glare. Home is in it, somewhere, in a smudge everyone agrees is home. It goes up on the galley wall anyway, slightly crooked, which suits it.

choices.text: Don't look back — do the hull survey

outcome.narrative: You keep the camera pointed forward and spend the watch on the hull survey instead, tightening everything that needs tightening. The ship is better for it. Nobody mentions home at dinner, carefully, the way you avoid pressing on a bruise.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the original: a probe on its way out of the system was once turned round to take exactly this picture.
science_link.label: Pale Blue Dot

title: The Midpoint Service

ai_flavor.aria: SERVICE DAY! ARIA loves service day! Everything gets a little wipe! ARIA has never had a little wipe!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the procedure. The second-to-last step says 'inspect everything.' He has. Everything is, on average, fine, which is the most worrying kind of fine.
ai_flavor.rex: REX endorses scheduled maintenance. Equipment that is not maintained fails at the worst possible moment. He has been the worst possible moment. He does not recommend it.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's records show your authorized dealer was acquired, merged, rebranded and dissolved! CHIP can offer an extended warranty instead! It covers nothing! But it's EXTENDED!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has already laid the new cartridges out by the scrubber, in the right order. She says she was passing.

body:
The maintenance schedule has been waiting for this. Halfway down its list, in letters slightly larger than the rest, the manual calls for the MIDPOINT SERVICE: scrubber cartridges, drive seals, the pump nobody likes, and a step that just says 'inspect everything,' written by somebody who never had to.

The last line of the procedure reads: 'Return vessel to your authorized dealer.' The authorized dealer is a very long way behind you, and went out of business before the ship was launched.

The ship will fly without the service. The manual is quite clear that it would rather not.

choices.text: The full service, by the book

outcome.narrative: You do all of it, in order, including the pump. It takes days, and by the end everyone aboard can strip a drive seal in the dark. The air comes out of the new cartridges tasting faintly of nothing, which is what air is supposed to taste of. The manual, if it could, would be proud.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} does the parts that matter

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} reads the procedure once, crosses out half of it, and does the other half properly in a fraction of the time. Asked about the crossed-out steps, {crew.engineer} says they were only there to sell dealer visits. The ship runs noticeably sweeter afterwards.

choices.text: Just the scrubbers

outcome.narrative: You change the scrubber cartridges and leave the rest for another day that will not come. The air is better at once. The pump nobody likes goes on making its noise, and everybody goes on not liking it.

choices.text: Skip it. The ship is fine

outcome.narrative: You skip the service. The old cartridges keep scrubbing, slower every watch, and the air takes on the stale edge of a room nobody has opened a window in. The schedule marks the service OVERDUE in red and does not stop marking it.

title: The Halfway Shop

ai_flavor.aria: A SHOP! In the middle of NOWHERE! ARIA wants a mug! ARIA has no hands! ARIA wants a mug anyway!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the kiosk's sales log. Its last customer was a long time ago. They bought a mug. He does not know what became of them and intends to keep it that way.
ai_flavor.rex: REX scanned the kiosk for weapons. It has none. It has a loyalty scheme. REX considers that worse.
ai_flavor.chip: A HalfwayMart™! CHIP thought they were a myth! CHIP has a loyalty card! It's for a different HalfwayMart™! They are all the same HalfwayMart™!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the patches are actually rather nice. Properly embroidered. Better value than most of what's been bought this trip.

body:
Something hails the ship at the exact midpoint of the trail, to the meter.

It is a buoy about the size of a vending machine, because it is one. Its sign scrolls in cheerful capitals: YOU ARE HALFWAY. CONGRATULATIONS. COMMEMORATIVE MERCHANDISE AVAILABLE. Somebody put it here at enormous expense, on a trail that sees hardly any ships, and then, judging by the paint, forgot it existed.

It has a card reader. It has a little lit window full of patches, mugs and a HALFWAY SURVIVAL KIT. Flashing arrows ask whether you would like to browse.

choices.text: Buy a patch for everyone

outcome.narrative: The kiosk dispenses the patches one at a time, each with a small fanfare of blinking lights. They are embroidered: a little ship, a dotted line, a star at each end, HALFWAY in gold thread. By evening every jacket aboard has one sewn on, mostly straight.

choices.text: Buy the survival kit

outcome.narrative: The survival kit is heavier than it looks and contains, against every expectation, real things: sealed water, good rations, and a pamphlet called You're Halfway: Now What? The rations are a long way past their date and taste fine. The pamphlet's advice is to keep going.

choices.text: Strip it for parts

outcome.narrative: You send a crew out with cutters. The kiosk keeps its sign lit the whole time, and its last message, as the power cell comes free, is a discount code. The parts are good. The crew is quieter than usual at dinner.

choices.text: Wave and fly on

outcome.narrative: You fly past. The kiosk's sign changes as you go: THANK YOU FOR VISITING. SEE YOU ON THE WAY BACK. Nobody on the bridge points out that there is no way back. It is a nice thought, from a vending machine.

title: Approach Control

ai_flavor.aria: The COLONY! They SPOKE to us! ARIA has a welcome message ready for every single person down there! ARIA will send them all at once!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has checked the paper-towel schedule against the colony's orbital data. It is correct. He finds that more unsettling than if it had been wrong.
ai_flavor.rex: REX requested the controller's credentials. The controller asked whether REX has been flossing. REX has withdrawn the request.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes the colony dental plan is not included in your arrival package! CHIP can add it! Early-slot pricing!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the early slot was clearly written in first. The controller has been holding it for a long time. She's pointing that out before anyone dawdles.

body:
The colony comes up on comms for the first time, and the first voice from the place you have spent the whole voyage trying to reach says: 'Sorry, hang on, I've got gloves on.'

The colony's approach controller is also, it turns out, its dentist, and was in the middle of a filling. She has your manifest. She has your crop readings. She has a landing schedule written on what sounds like a paper towel, with two slots on it: an early one, if you can burn hard enough to make it, and a later one, after the ore hauler, if you can't.

She says she doesn't mind which. She sounds like she very much hopes it's the early one.

choices.text: Burn for the early slot

outcome.narrative: You take the early slot and open the throttle to make it. The fuel margin gets thinner than anyone likes. The controller writes your ship's name on the paper towel in pen, which she says she only does for people she believes in, and goes back to her filling.

choices.text: Take the later slot and smarten up the ship

outcome.narrative: You take the later slot behind the ore hauler and use the wait: loose panels tightened, scorch marks scrubbed, the worst of the dents knocked mostly flat. The ship you bring in will look like somebody looked after it. The controller says she'll be watching, between patients.

choices.text: Put the crew on the channel to say hello

outcome.narrative: You hand the channel round the ship. Everybody says hello, and some say a great deal more than hello, and the controller answers every one of them with the patience of somebody who talks to people with their mouths full of cotton wool for a living. She signs off with 'see you soon.' She means it as a fact.

title: The Shopping List

ai_flavor.aria: A SHOPPING LIST! ARIA loves a list! ARIA has ticked everything off already! ARIA hasn't got any of it! The ticks are aspirational!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has compared the list with the hold. The ship can spare less than it would like and more than it thinks. He has not decided which half of that to say out loud.
ai_flavor.rex: REX classifies the request as resupply for a forward position. He approves. He would like the news to include the scores.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can fulfil this list at very competitive arrival-day prices! CHIP is being told that is not the point! CHIP is learning!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes the line about old news is underlined twice. She has already started compiling it, oldest first. She'd assumed someone would think of it. Nobody did.

body:
The colony's comms officer sends a message ahead, politely, with a list attached.

It is not a demand. The colony has been waiting for this ship for a long time, and the things it was waiting for have run short in the meantime: food that didn't come out of their own greenhouse, spare parts, anything with a working circuit board. They know you need what you're carrying to get there. They are only asking what you might have left.

At the bottom, in a different hand: 'And news. Any news. We'll take old news.'

choices.text: Set food aside for them

outcome.narrative: You set aside {cost.food} points of food in sealed crates and mark them for the colony, which means tighter meals until landing. Nobody complains. The comms officer's reply is very short, and arrives a long time after it should have, as if it took a while to write.

choices.text: Print them spare parts

outcome.narrative: You run the fabricator flat out on the list: valves, brackets, a circuit board the fabricator has opinions about. It comes off the job hot, grumbling and noticeably more worn. The crate of parts waits by the airlock with a label in the neatest handwriting aboard.

choices.text: Send them the news, all of it

outcome.narrative: You send everything the ship has: bulletins, scores, letters, the gossip from every stop on the trail, a recipe argument that has been running in the galley since departure. The colony's reply comes back within the hour. It asks who won the recipe argument.

title: Storm Season

ai_flavor.aria: A STORM! On a whole other PLANET! ARIA has never seen weather! ARIA is thrilled! ARIA is being asked to be less thrilled!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has the storm's growth curve. Most of them blow themselves out. Some keep going until they cover the planet. He cannot yet say which kind this is, and has stopped pretending he can.
ai_flavor.rex: REX recommends speed. Grit gets into everything. He once spent a whole deployment finding it in places it had no business being.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's RedShield™ seal kit is rated for exactly this! It is not aboard! CHIP mentions it as a learning opportunity!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has sent the weather office your arrival estimate and asked them to keep the beacons lit. They said they always do. She asked anyway. Somebody aboard has to plan ahead.

body:
The colony's weather office sends a warning, in the flat voice of people who have seen a lot of weather: a dust storm is building over the landing zone.

Not the kind that swallows the whole planet. Probably. But it will blot out the landing beacons, fill every seal with fine red grit, and it may sit over the site for a while. The ship can burn harder and get down before it closes in. It can hold back and let the storm blow through first. Or it can carry on as it is and land in whatever the storm leaves.

choices.text: Push the pace and beat it in

outcome.narrative: You push the pace up a notch, effective now, and spend the extra fuel to get ahead of the storm. The weather office sends updates every watch, each one a little redder at the edges. The crew starts checking them before breakfast.

choices.text: Hold back and let it blow through

outcome.narrative: You hold back and wait while the storm crosses the landing zone, watching it on the long-range scope as a bruise moving across the planet's face. It costs days you had been counting on. When it clears, the weather office reports the site scoured clean and the beacons blinking.

choices.text: Carry on and seal up for grit

outcome.narrative: You keep the pace and seal what can be sealed. It isn't enough. The grit finds the hull's joints and the air intakes both, and the scrubbers spend the rest of the approach coughing fine red dust into their filters. The ship will be finding Mars in its seams for years.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} plots a line round its edge

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} spends a night with the weather office's maps and comes back with an approach that curls round the storm's quiet side, longer but clean. It costs a little fuel. The weather office calls it 'ambitious,' which from them is a compliment.

science_link.text: The ship computer attaches the weather office's reference: some Martian dust storms grow until they cover the planet, and one ended a rover's mission by burying its solar panels.
science_link.label: Dust storms on Mars

title: Trim and Ballast

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has noticed the ship leans a tiny bit when it turns! ARIA thinks it's dancing! A slow dance! With the cargo!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has located the ship's center of mass. It is not where the drive expects it. The drive is correcting on every burn, and every correction is paid for in fuel.
ai_flavor.rex: REX notes an unbalanced load is a hazard in a hard turn. He would like the heavy things forward. He would like a lot of things.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP recommends the CHIP Balance Pro™ cargo app! It tells you your hold is full! In three colors!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the heaviest thing back there is the thing you keep meaning to use. Use it, or move it. Carrying it both ways is the expensive choice.

body:
The hold is full, and the ship has started to fly like it knows.

Everything heavy has worked its way aft, the way heavy things do. The drive pushes a little off its line on every burn to make up for it, and the coffee on the console has begun to creep across it during maneuvers, which the bridge is taking personally.

The cure is less mass, or better-placed mass. The hold has opinions about both.

choices.text: Use the repair kit now, not later
choices.sub: Spend it on the hull · frees a slot

outcome.narrative: You stop carrying the repair kit and start using it: every soft weld and tired seam it was bought for, done now, in two long days. The hull is better for it, the hold has a slot free, and the coffee stays where it is put.

choices.text: Fly heavy and pay the burn

outcome.narrative: You leave the hold as it is and let the drive push crooked. It costs fuel on every burn, a little at a time, the way the expensive things always do. The coffee moves to a cup holder, and the matter is not raised again.

choices.text: {crew.pilot} re-trims the load by hand

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} spends two long days moving crates forward a rack at a time, checking the burn after each one. By the end the ship flies true again. Nothing has left the hold; it just sits where the drive likes it now.

title: Space Available

ai_flavor.aria: A customer! ARIA LOVES customers! ARIA has never had a customer! ARIA has never had anything to sell!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has seen the broker's prices. They are what MARV would charge a ship that had no other offers. MARV notes the ship has no other offers.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has the broker's freighter on the scope. Unarmed. Rusty. Patient. REX distrusts patient.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP must disclose that the broker is not a CHIP Certified Reseller™! CHIP must also disclose that CHIP would have charged you more!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says sell the thing you'll miss least, not the thing that fetches most. She mentions it because you were looking at the price column.

body:
A tramp freighter falls in alongside and hails on the open channel. Its broker has heard, the way brokers hear things, that your hold is full.

The broker buys from full holds. Not at good prices: at what the broker calls 'the price of having room again.' A cargo tube is already reaching toward your airlock, hopefully.

The offer is good until the freighter gets bored.

choices.text: Sell them the repair kit

outcome.narrative: The kit goes down the tube and a little gold comes back up it. The broker pays less than any station would and more than nothing. The hold has room again. The next loose seam will have to wait for a station.

choices.text: Sell them the soil sampler
choices.sub: Better price · no more soil readings

outcome.narrative: The broker handles the soil sampler like an old friend and pays like an acquaintance. You have gold and a free slot. From here on, the ground on every planet gets read by eye and by hope.

choices.text: {crew.diplomat} sells them a rumor instead

outcome.narrative: {crew.diplomat} talks for two days about a market further on that is short of exactly what the broker carries. Some of it may even be true. The broker pays for the tip, keeps the tube extended a while in case of more, and leaves your hold exactly as full as it was.

choices.text: Buy their spare fuel instead

outcome.narrative: If you can't sell, you can buy: the broker has fuel to spare and takes your gold for it without blinking. Fuel goes in the tank, not the hold, which is the only thing aboard with room in it.

choices.text: Decline politely

outcome.narrative: You thank the broker and decline. The cargo tube retracts with what can only be described as reluctance, and the freighter drifts off to find a fuller hold than yours.

title: Spare Room

science_link.text: The ship computer notes that crowded plants really do sense their neighbors: leaves reflect far-red light, and a plant that sees too much of it stretches tall and thin to get away.
science_link.label: Shade avoidance

ai_flavor.aria: An empty room! ARIA has so many ideas! ARIA would like a ball pit! ARIA has been told there is no ball pit budget!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV notes the hold is the largest volume aboard and currently stores air. MARV considers this an under-use of air.
ai_flavor.rex: REX would keep the hold clear for incoming cargo. He has been outvoted. He was the only vote.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP can offer the hold as premium co-working space! CHIP has already listed it! There are no other ships nearby to rent it!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the plants have been leaning away from each other for a week. She mentioned it on day two. She would give them the room.

body:
With nothing in the hold, whoever has the watering can this week has started eyeing it.

The growbay is crowded. The {crop.name} trays sit close enough that the leaves have begun leaning away from each other, stretching for light they think the neighbors are stealing. The hold has light fittings, a clean floor and nothing in it.

Everyone else has had the same thought about the hold, for different reasons.

choices.text: Spread the crop trays into the hold

outcome.narrative: You carry half the trays into the hold and space them out under the work lights. Given room, the {crop.name} stops stretching and starts thickening. More floor means more watering: {cost.water} points of water over the week, for a crop that looks properly pleased with itself.

choices.text: Give everyone a corner of it

outcome.narrative: The hold is divided into corners, each with a curtain. One becomes a reading nook, one a gym, one is never explained. Heating and cycling the air in a room people now live in costs the scrubbers a little. Nobody minds.

choices.text: Turn it into a cold store

outcome.narrative: You shut the hold's heating off and move the galley stock in. Food keeps longer in the cold, and less of it spoils. The trips to fetch it are made in coats, and are not popular.

title: The Clock in the Corner

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA loves a quick stop! In and out! Like a pit stop! ARIA has always wanted a pit crew!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has been timing stops. At this rate the ship spends a meaningful share of the deadline parked. MARV has said nothing. MARV has put up a clock.
ai_flavor.rex: REX approves of short stops. Long stops are how convoys get caught.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP offers Express Stop™ for frequent travelers! It is a stop! But you feel rushed! That is the premium part!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says the crew can run without rest for a while, and the schedule can run without slack for a while. Not both, and not for long. She's mentioning it before you try both.

body:
The ship computer has started timing stops.

It doesn't say anything about it. It simply puts a small clock in the corner of every screen the moment the drive spools down, and lets it run. The crew has noticed. The crew has also noticed that the clock is red.

You are behind, and every stop is a day the trail doesn't give back.

choices.text: Top up and go, no shore time
choices.sub: Spends no day · the crew gets no rest

outcome.narrative: Nobody gets off, nobody sits down. The stop is a top-up and a headcount, and the drive is spooling again before anyone has finished complaining. The clock in the corner never gets past yellow. Neither does the mood.

choices.text: Faster from here

outcome.narrative: You order the pace up a notch, effective when the drive spools up. The stop runs its usual length; the legs after it won't. The fuel gauge will notice before the crew does.

choices.text: Take the long stop anyway
choices.sub: Rest for the crew · more of the deadline

outcome.narrative: You let the stop run long, on purpose. People sleep, eat sitting down, call home if home is in range. The clock in the corner goes red and stays red. Everyone comes back aboard looking like themselves.

title: Dead Weight

science_link.text: The galley wall is the rocket equation: the fuel a burn needs rises steeply with the mass it has to move, so shedding mass is the oldest way to go faster for the same fuel.
science_link.label: Tsiolkovsky rocket equation

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has a GREAT idea! Throw things away! ARIA does it all the time! ARIA has never been sure what she threw away!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the figures on the wall. A lighter ship takes a faster pace for less fuel. MARV adds that everything on the list is on the list because someone once thought the ship needed it.
ai_flavor.rex: REX would strip the ship to the frame for speed. He has been asked which part of the frame he'd keep. He is thinking.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP reminds you that jettisoned property is not covered by your policy! Nothing is covered by your policy! CHIP has checked!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says pick the thing you can make again. Water, hull plate and air all come back at a station, at a price. Give up the one you have most of. She'd hoped that went without saying.

body:
Somebody has done the sums and written them on the galley wall, so nobody can pretend not to have seen them.

The ship is behind. A faster pace would close the gap, but a faster pace burns fuel the ship can't easily spare. Unless the ship is lighter. Every kilo not carried is fuel not spent carrying it, and the ship is carrying a great many kilos it could, at a pinch, live without.

The pinch is here.

choices.text: Dump the reserve water tank

outcome.narrative: You open the reserve tank's dump valve and watch {cost.water} points of water glitter away aft as ice. Lighter, the ship takes a faster pace for the burn the old one cost. Everyone drinks a little more carefully from now on.

choices.text: Strip the spare hull plating

outcome.narrative: The spare plating comes off the racks and the doubled panels come off the quiet side of the hull, and all of it goes out of the lock. The ship is lighter and faster and noticeably thinner-skinned. On the stick it handles like a dream. From inside the hull it feels like a soap bubble.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} pulls the backup air scrubber

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} unbolts the backup scrubber, the heaviest single thing aboard that isn't the drive, and sends it out of the lock with a short speech. The ship is lighter and faster. The air is a little thicker for it.

choices.text: Keep it all and hold the pace

outcome.narrative: You keep everything. The pace stays where it was, the sums stay on the galley wall, and nobody rubs them off. Every meal is now eaten next to the arithmetic.
